context: dry-room factory · electrode, cell assembly and formation; dry rooms and utilities are the hard part

brief.intro: New to this project type? A battery cell factory makes lithium-ion cells in three stages. Electrode manufacturing mixes active powders into a slurry, coats it onto metal foil, dries it in long ovens and presses and slits it. Cell assembly cuts, stacks or winds the electrodes, puts them in a case, fills in the electrolyte and seals the cell. Formation then charges and discharges every cell for the first time and lets it rest for days in large racked halls. Lithium reacts with moisture, so assembly happens in dry rooms where the air is hundreds of times drier than a desert — and making that air takes an enormous utility plant. The building is big but ordinary; the dry rooms, the solvent-recovery system, the power demand of formation and the fire protection are what make it hard.

scope.desc: Coating machines with long drying ovens and solvent (NMP) recovery.

scope.desc: Notching, stacking or winding, welding, casing, electrolyte filling and sealing.

scope.desc: Dehumidifiers, chillers, boilers, NMP recovery, nitrogen and bulk chemicals.

scope.name: Plant utilities
scope.desc: Chilled water & large chillers, Steam / hot water, Compressed dry air & nitrogen, NMP solvent recovery — the services every machine needs before it can run.

scope.name: Power supply & control
scope.desc: Substation, transformers, switchgear, cabling and the plant control system.

scope.name: Fire protection, HVAC & dust / fume extraction
scope.desc: Life-safety and environmental systems required for the operating permit.

scope.name: Commissioning & ramp-up
scope.desc: Line-by-line acceptance, first cells, formation and ageing (weeks), customer qualification of cells, then ramp-up.

glossary.plain: the coated foil — cathode or anode — that stores the energy.
the paste of active material, binder and solvent that is coated onto the foil.
the solvent used for cathode slurry; it is evaporated in the ovens and recovered.
pressing the coated foil between rolls to the exact thickness and density.
a sealed room kept at a very low dew point so moisture cannot reach the cell materials.
the measure of how dry the air is; dry rooms run at about −40 °C or lower.
the first controlled charging of a cell, which creates its internal protective layer.
resting the cells for days or weeks after formation to find weak ones.
the share of cells that pass; raising it is the main work of ramp-up.

must_get_right: Utilities lead: dehumidifiers, chillers and power must be running before the dry rooms can be proven, and the dry rooms must be proven before assembly equipment is unpacked.
Size and order the power supply early — formation and the dry-room plant make this one of the most power-hungry factories there is.
Formation and ageing mean the first cells take weeks to come out; customer qualification then takes months. Put both between 'first cell' and 'production'.
Fire strategy (formation halls, electrolyte, finished cells) shapes the building and the insurer's approval — settle it at design stage.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Building and utility plant → power-on → dry rooms built and proven → equipment move-in and installation → site acceptance tests → first electrodes → first cells → formation and ageing → qualification → ramp-up. The critical path runs through power and utilities to the dry-room acceptance, or through the equipment delivery.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: power supply, dry rooms not reaching dew point, late equipment, low yield at start-up, and long customer qualification. Contingency is held before first cell and before start of deliveries.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
